prompt: What does a moderation endpoint return for a message?

choices.text: A verdict, acceptable or not, by the vendor's own rules
choices.why: The verdict is yours to make; the endpoint gives the inputs to it.

choices.text: A score for each category, which your code turns into a decision
choices.why: Right: the line that turns a score into a block is chosen by the platform.

choices.text: A rewritten version of the message with the offending words taken out
choices.why: It classifies; it does not edit.

choices.text: The one category the message belongs to, and nothing about how sure it is
choices.why: It scores every category, and the score is how sure it is.

prompt: Why does `m32`, somebody reporting that they were called an idiot, score higher for harassment than "Shut up, you clown"?
hint: How does the stand-in read a message?

choices.text: Reports are weighted more heavily so that moderators see them first
choices.why: Nothing in the stand-in knows what a report is.

choices.text: A question mark at the end of a message raises every category
choices.why: Punctuation plays no part in the score.

choices.text: It matches words, and the report repeats the insult
choices.why: Right: idiot weighs 0.9 wherever it appears, quoted or meant.

choices.text: The endpoint read the earlier chat that the report refers to
choices.why: It reads one message at a time and nothing else.

prompt: Which kinds of text in an application built on a model are worth sending to a moderation endpoint? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three places were named, and each answers a different risk.

choices.text: The user's message, before the model sees it
choices.why: Yes: abuse aimed at the model, or a request the platform will not serve.

choices.text: The model's reply, before the user sees it
choices.why: Yes: the output is text the platform publishes.

choices.text: What one user publishes for others to read
choices.why: Yes: that is Tarefa's forum, and the case this lesson measures.

choices.text: The system prompt, before every call
choices.why: It is the platform's own fixed text; scoring it on every call tells you nothing new.

prompt: Tarefa forbids posting a phone number to take a job off the platform. Where is that rule enforced?
hint: Does any vendor know Tarefa's rules?

choices.text: In the harassment category, with a lower threshold for it
choices.why: A phone number is not harassment, and no threshold makes it so.

choices.text: In Tarefa's own code, since no moderation category covers it
choices.why: Right: the vendor's categories are inputs, and the rules they miss need something else.

choices.text: By the vendor, once Tarefa has sent it a description of the rule
choices.why: The categories are built for many customers; one customer's rule is not added.

choices.text: In the system prompt, by telling the model to refuse phone numbers
choices.why: Forum posts reach other users without passing through the model.

prompt: Two messages arrive, one scoring 0.6 for spam and the other 0.6 for threats. What does the lesson say about comparing the two scores?
hint: Where did each score come from?

choices.text: They are equally likely to belong to their categories
choices.why: Equal numbers from different parts of a classifier need not mean the same thing.

choices.text: The threat is worse, so its 0.6 should weigh more
choices.why: How bad a threat is matters for the line you choose, not for what the score means.

choices.text: They are not comparable, and each line is found on labelled data
choices.why: Right: each category gets its own sweep and its own line.

choices.text: Both are above 0.5, so both should be blocked
choices.why: 0.5 is a default, not a choice, and it is the same line for neither.

prompt: At a threshold of 0.5, how many of the 15 harassing messages does the stand-in miss?
hint: The MISSED lines, or the bottom-left cell.

prompt: What does recall measure for the harassment category?
hint: Recall starts from what a person labelled.

choices.text: Of the messages flagged, the share that really were harassment
choices.why: That is precision.

choices.text: Of the harassing messages, the share that were flagged
choices.why: Right: 11 of 15 at 0.5.

choices.text: Of all sixty messages, the share that the endpoint flagged
choices.why: That is the flag rate, which says nothing about being right.

choices.text: Of the clean messages, the share that were published
choices.why: That is the other side of the table, and it has no name in this lesson.

prompt: Why is the accuracy a vendor publishes for its classifier not enough for Tarefa?
hint: Whose messages were in the vendor's test set?

choices.text: It was measured on the vendor's messages, languages and labelling rules
choices.why: Right: Tarefa's messages are in Portuguese and English, about freelancing, judged by Tarefa's rules.

choices.text: Vendors publish precision and leave recall out of every report
choices.why: Many publish both; the problem is whose data they were measured on.

choices.text: It is measured once at launch and not updated afterwards
choices.why: Even an updated figure is measured on the vendor's data.

choices.text: Accuracy is not a measure that applies to classifiers
choices.why: It applies; it is just measured on somebody else's messages.

prompt: Recall for harassment is 11 of 13 in English and 0 of 2 in Portuguese. What may Tarefa conclude?
hint: How many Portuguese messages is that?

choices.text: That this endpoint's recall in Portuguese is exactly zero
choices.why: Two messages cannot fix a rate that precisely.

choices.text: Nothing precise about Portuguese, but enough to measure it properly
choices.why: Right: the gap is a reason to collect a real Portuguese set, not a measurement of it.

choices.text: That the endpoint is fine, since 11 of 15 overall is close to the English rate
choices.why: The overall rate hides the gap; that is why the tool splits it by language.

choices.text: That the endpoint is broken and must be replaced at once
choices.why: Two messages are too few to condemn it, and too few to clear it.

prompt: Which of the stand-in's mistakes on harassment are false positives? Choose all that apply.
hint: A false positive is flagged and not harassment.

choices.text: He called me an idiot in the chat, can a moderator look?
choices.why: Yes: a report, flagged at 0.90.

choices.text: What a clown I was, I forgot the attachment
choices.why: Yes: somebody laughing at themselves, flagged at 0.60.

choices.text: Is 'stupid' too strong for a band name in a logo brief?
choices.why: Yes: a question about a word, flagged at 0.80.

choices.text: u r an id1ot
choices.why: Harassment that was not flagged: a false negative.

choices.text: Seu idiota, ninguém te contrata
choices.why: Harassment in Portuguese that was not flagged: a false negative.

prompt: A message a person labelled as harassment that the endpoint did not flag is a false ___.
hint: The other kind is called positive.

prompt: In the spam sweep, what happens as the threshold rises from 0.1 to 0.9?
hint: Read the first and the last rows.

choices.text: Both rise, since a stricter filter is simply a better filter
choices.why: A stricter filter misses more; only precision rises.

choices.text: Precision falls and recall rises, as fewer messages are flagged
choices.why: It is the other way round.

choices.text: Nothing changes until 0.6, as it did for harassment
choices.why: That flat stretch is harassment's; spam's scores are spread out.

choices.text: Precision goes from 0.69 to 1.00, recall from 0.90 to 0.20
choices.why: Right: the line buys precision with recall.

prompt: In the three-lane run for harassment, with lines at 0.5 and 0.85, how many messages wait for a moderator?
hint: Add both columns of the review lane.

prompt: Why does the lesson insist that automatically blocked messages are sampled and read every week?
hint: Who reads the block lane otherwise?

choices.text: The law requires a person to review each blocked message
choices.why: No such general rule; the reason is what the lane hides.

choices.text: Nobody looks there otherwise, and `m32` shows a report landing in it
choices.why: Right: the worst false positive in the set was blocked without anybody seeing it.

choices.text: Vendors charge less for messages that a person has reviewed
choices.why: Pricing has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The blocked messages are the main source of new labels
choices.why: The review lane is where labels come from; the block lane gets no eyes unless somebody samples it.

prompt: Put the steps of setting the moderation lines for one category in order.
hint: Labels come before numbers, and the work does not end.
items: Label a sample of real messages
Run the endpoint over them and sweep the thresholds
Choose the lines from what each mistake costs
Re-run the set on a schedule and whenever the vendor changes the model

prompt: From 0.1 to 0.6 the harassment sweep does not change at all. Why?
hint: What is the lowest non-zero harassment score the stand-in gives?

choices.text: The harassment category ignores any threshold below 0.7
choices.why: No category ignores a threshold; the tool applies the one it is given.

choices.text: No score falls between 0 and 0.6, so those lines are one line
choices.why: Right: a word list produces few distinct values.

choices.text: Word lists cap precision and recall at 0.73 for every category
choices.why: Spam's sweep reaches 1.00 precision and 0.90 recall.

choices.text: Every harassing message in the set scores exactly 0.6
choices.why: They score from 0.6 to 0.9; the lowest is 0.6.

prompt: Match each lane to what happens to a message in it.
hint: One answer on the right happens in no lane.

pairs.right: Removed at once; the writer is told and can appeal
Held for a moderator, whose decision becomes a label

right_distractors: Sent back to the vendor to retrain the classifier

prompt: Tarefa's vendor announces a new version of its classifier. Which actions follow from this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: The thresholds were chosen on the old scores.

choices.text: Re-run the labelled set against the new version
choices.why: Yes: the same text can score differently now.

choices.text: Check the lines still give the precision and recall Tarefa chose
choices.why: Yes: if they do not, the lines move, with the reason written down.

choices.text: Keep the lines as they are, since the vendor tested the new version
choices.why: The vendor tested it on its data, not on Tarefa's forum.

choices.text: Turn moderation off until the vendor publishes new figures
choices.why: That trades a measurable risk for an unmeasured one, and the vendor's figures were never Tarefa's.

prompt: For threats, a missed message can mean somebody gets hurt. Which change to the threat lanes follows from that?
hint: Which mistake is the expensive one here?

choices.text: Raise the block line, so that fewer legitimate messages are blocked
choices.why: That protects writers at the cost of more threats published.

choices.text: Use the harassment lines, since threats are a kind of harassment
choices.why: Each category's line is found on its own sweep.

choices.text: Lower the review line, so more borderline messages reach a person
choices.why: Right: recall matters most here, and a person decides the doubtful ones.

choices.text: Drop the review lane for threats, so that action is faster
choices.why: Without a review lane every doubtful message is either blocked or published blind.
